The Stars Come Down, we get that rare thing, a family drama about the white working-class today, with ramifications for us all...
A cracking evening, very funny and wholly recommended.
Steel’s writing in her best play yet.
Beth Steel’s debut for the National…plunges us into the middle of a clan whose passions, jokes and prejudices are utterly authentic.
I loved its sweaty honesty, its big, generous canvas, its energy and its deep sympathy for its characters.
Bijan Sheibani's lively, loving, in-the-round production revels in the earthy humour of Steel's script, which instantly convinces in its depiction of family dynamics.
It’s a gloriously messy affair, compassionate, hilarious, and tangy with fear and longing.
Steel’s play still feels like an achievement, deftly handling a huge line-up of Northern working-class characters and making them shine with a sharp, flawed brightness.
So even if Steel leaves it all hanging, it's still one helluva bittersweet ride.
'Till the Stars Come Down' is a funny, heartbreaking piece of writing, wonderfully acted, tenderly directed... except when it isn't.
The strength of individual characterisations elevates the drama from a mere cacophony of emotions and it is further driven by raw truth and an unending stream of hilariously dumped one-liners.
Their warmth, their subtlety and their ability to portray a family in love and at war make this rewarding, utterly unmissable play a theatrical event to remember.
Beth Steel makes an early bid for play of the year with the properly funny, fiercely loving and piercingly perceptive Till the Stars Come Down.
Bijan Sheibani’s direction welds it all together making it a delight without blunting its political point.
All told, I thought Till the Stars Come Down was a truly fascinating and entertaining show.
A fine ending to a sometimes crass and ill-disciplined show.
Till the Stars Come Down, her new play at The National Theatre, is a sparkling bundle of light and luminous love.
If you can forgive the stereotyping, and the late arrival of heartbreak, this is a great night out which — whatever my doubts about its populism — will surely scoop awards.
Even this early, it’s safe to predict we’ll look back at the end of 2024 and proclaim it as one of the year’s finest.
Beth Steel’s writing is a firework show, sparkling as any sitcom but artful, gradually drawing out differences and family bonds, preparing us for conflagration later.
Till The Stars Come Down is another exceptional show from National Theatre, more than matching the incredible quality of their productions last year.
Nevertheless, while the wedding might be a disaster, the show is a triumph.
Steel always roots the politics in the personal and while there's a lot going on here she pulls off the theatrical magic trick of making you laugh, cry and think on one big night out.
Beth Steel's beautifully observed play hones in on the relationship between Sylvia, her two sisters and their Aunty Carol.
This show is a tour de force in which everyone involved seemed to be at the very top of their game.
Steel’s play is a fascinating alternative, a way into similar narratives but entirely from the perspective of its female characters...

cn.t: Critics hail Beth Steel's working-class wedding drama as hilarious yet heartbreaking, with authentic characters and sharp writing that evokes Chekhov. A few find it occasionally overstuffed, but most praise its emotional depth and vivid portrayal of post-industrial Britain.

vr.q: I give till the stars come down four stars and all praise to the National Theater for presenting it
